Before we open the numbers, one comment on how to read them. The baseline for this comparison is the twelve months before the rollout, not the calendar year, so the uplift you see in the second column is a like for like figure. The margin improvement of four point two percent is aggregate. At category level the range is wide: two categories carried almost all of it, and three moved backwards. My advice is to look at the trajectory rather than the single number. A four percent improvement in one quarter that comes from one category is not a trend. It is a data point with a good story attached to it.

One thing before your presentation tomorrow. You have the numbers, and they are strong, but do not open with them. In my experience, the moment you say four point two percent, half the room starts checking whether they believe the number, and nobody listens to the next three sentences. Open with the question instead. Tell them what you were trying to find out, then give the baseline, then the result. And when you get to the result, give one number, not five. If they want the granularity, they will ask, and then you can disaggregate it in front of them. That is a much stronger position than defending a table.

First, the analyst defines the baseline for the comparison. Then she measures the uplift against that baseline. After that, she checks the trajectory over four quarters. Next, she disaggregates the aggregate figure by category. Finally, she presents one number to the board and keeps the granularity for the questions.
